Space Closure in Incisor Protrusion Problems

I Sliding vs Loop Mechanics

  • Sliding: significant resistance to sliding — binding + friction (big disadvantage) — but automatic generation of root-paralleling moments at the extraction site (big advantage).
  • Loop: no frictional resistance (big advantage), but the loop must be adjusted to generate a root-paralleling moment kept in proportion to the closing force (extra work/complexity).

Sliding Mechanics

  • The rectangular wire on which sliding occurs must be undersized relative to the bracket yet strong enough not to bend under force. The closer the wire–bracket contact, the greater the friction. Because slots run slightly large and wires slightly small, even a full-dimension wire has clearance.
  • A 3-mil (0.5 mm) wire-to-slot difference largely eliminates friction (binding still present). The usual undersized-wire/oversized-slot combo means a nominal 2-mil clearance is adequate — 16 × 25 in an 18-slot is acceptable; 19 × 25 in a 22-slot is better (excellent strength, rarely bends).
  • Both a force (to move the tooth) and a moment (to prevent tipping) are needed Fig 16.1. Wider brackets lower binding and generate root-paralleling moments — but too wide compromises alignment; the best compromise is tooth-specific brackets ~half the tooth width.
  • A-NiTi superelastic coil springs are the ideal force source (known, near-constant magnitude). Elastomeric chains decay rapidly between visits (less ideal, but easier placement + better hygiene). Sliding closure has excellent fail-safe characteristics.
  • When maxillary incisors protrude, torque in the incisor brackets is often needed during retraction to keep them from becoming too upright — the reciprocal is a forward force on the posterior anchorage Fig 16.3.
Links Ch 9 The mechanics of friction/binding and the force-vs-couple balance for bodily movement are detailed in Chapter 9 — "not all moments in sliding closure are so automatic that they need no thought."

Closing Loop Mechanics

Performance is set by three things: its spring properties, the moment it generates, and its location relative to adjacent brackets. The frictionless design can reduce anchorage problems and shorten closure time. (Closing loops should also be made in rectangular wire to keep the wire from rolling in the slot.)

  • Spring properties Fig 16.4 depend almost entirely on the wire material (steel or TMA), wire size, and distance between attachments (mostly the amount of wire in the loop). Changing wire size produces the largest change. TMA (β-Ti) delivers about half the force of steel for any size/design. Springier wire / smaller cross-section → simpler loop designs.
  • Root-paralleling moments: a closing loop must generate a closing force and the moments to bring root apices together. The moment requirement limits how springy (how much wire) the loop can be. Placing wire horizontally rather than vertically improves moment delivery — so a loop only 7–8 mm tall but incorporating 10–12 mm+ of wire (delta-, L-, or T-shaped) is preferred Fig 16.5.
  • Parallel legs alone can't generate enough moment without an unacceptably tall loop, so add gable bends (40–45°) before insertion Fig 16.6.
  • Location: because of its gable bends the loop acts as a V-bend (position-sensitive). For fail-safe loops, place it at the spot that will be the center of the embrasure when the space is closed Fig 16.7 — in a first-premolar extraction, ~5 mm distal to the canine center (initially a one-third position; the moment on the premolar increases as closure proceeds — not ideal for maximum anchorage but unavoidable in a continuous arch).
  • Three additional design principles — fail-safe, simple, and activation method:
    • A loop must fail-safe — too much range/flexibility + broken appointments = disaster. Ideal: ~1 mm/month with no more than 2 mm of range before it locks up.
    • Simple beats complex (comfort, fabrication, breakage). Siatkowski's Opus loop elegantly gives near-constant moment-to-force ratios at variable activation Fig 16.8.
    • Activation: a loop is more effective closed than opened to activate — but a loop designed to be opened can lock (legs contact) when fully closed, giving the fail-safe. The opening-to-activate design is preferred (fail-safe outweighs the better spring quality).

II Bimaxillary Protrusion — Moderate Anchorage (50:50 / 60:40)

  • 22-slot: two-stage closure ≈ 60:40 (longer); en-masse sliding ≈ 50:50 at best. Two steps better control anchorage:
    • Stage 1 (canine retraction): slide along 18 × 25 or 19 × 25 steel with a NiTi spring/elastic ≈ 200 gm; a posterior stop in front of the first-molar tube incorporates everything except the canine into the anchor unit.
    • Stage 2 (incisor retraction): lower — slide on 18 × 25 or a T-loop in 18 × 25 steel; upper — a closing loop when more incisor torque is needed.
  • One-step segmented (retraction spring connecting stable bases Fig 16.10) is fastest but does not fail-safe (nothing maintains arch form/vertical if the spring distorts). A fail-safe one-step closure is also possible with 22-slot (as commonly done in 18-slot) — faster than two-stage, safer/simpler than segmented.
  • 18-slot: fits closing-loop principles well — an excellent loop is a delta loop in 16 × 22 steel, activated by opening (accurate activation, gable-bend moment, fails safe when fully closed). Hold the activated wire by bending the end gingivally behind the last tube, or a soldered tieback Fig 16.7. Reactivate gable bends after 3–4 mm of closure.

III Maximum Incisor Retraction (Maximum Anchorage)

  1. Stabilizing lingual arches — 36-mil or 32 × 32 steel (Burstone's removable designs preferred). Shift retraction:protraction to ~2:1. Avoid a palatal expansion loop unless specifically indicated (max rigidity wanted); lingual arches in finishing may impede final settling.
  2. Headgear + interarch elastics — extraoral force is transferred upper→lower via Class III elastics; can reach a 3:1 or 4:1 ratio.
  3. Two-step frictionless retraction — Gjessing's PG spring for canine retraction Fig 16.13, then closing loops (continuous or segmented) for incisors. Two problems: hard to control the canine in all three planes (needs both a root-paralleling and an anti-rotation gable bend), and segmental canine retraction is not fail-safe.
  4. Skeletal anchorage — the only way to close spaces totally by retracting the incisor–canine segment. Maxilla: screws in the palate stabilizing a TPA (indirect, force parallel to occlusal plane), or screws between 2nd premolar & 1st molar (up-and-back pull). Mandible: alveolar screws, ramus screws (invasive), or buccal-body screws (≈ palatal). Advantage: vertical + AP control; disadvantage: makes over-retraction possible.
Updated — RCT evidence Two RCTs found, surprisingly, that alveolar bone screws were no more effective than a Nance lingual arch at holding posterior anchorage — whereas palatal anchorage is now shown to be quite effective. So for maximum maxillary incisor retraction, indirect anchorage from screws in the anterior palate is now preferred.

IV Minimum Incisor Retraction

  1. Incorporate as many teeth as possible in the anterior anchor unit (reinforced anchorage).
  2. Place active lingual root torque in the incisor section Fig 16.3 (stationary anchorage).
  3. Break down posterior anchorage — move posteriors forward one tooth at a time (combine with added anterior torque).
  4. Skeletal anchorage — bone screws in the canine region are the easiest, most effective way to bring posteriors forward (especially when one side needs more than the other).
Class II Correction in Adolescents

I Differential Growth (growth modification + comprehensive treatment)

  • Girls mature earlier — often past the spurt before the full permanent dentition/comprehensive treatment can begin. Boys mature later with a longer spurt — more likely to have useful AP growth in the early permanent dentition.
  • A removable functional is unlikely to succeed in the early permanent dentition (must be modified/discontinued when fixed appliances start). Headgear — and most fixed functionals — are far more compatible with fixed appliances. The Herbst effectively corrects Class II molars (differential growth + forward displacement of mandibular teeth). For patients whose lower incisors are already at their forward limit, headgear is effective and introduces no Class II elastics effect (no flaring).

Headgear for Adolescent Growth Modification

  • Ideal patient: a 12–14-yr-old boy with Class II whose skeletal maturity is behind his dental development. (Boys at 13 ≈ girls at 11 — AP growth almost always continuing; girls at 13 ≈ boys at 15 — useful jaw change unlikely.)
  • If force is applied to the first molar, the premolars follow → consolidate space at a single location with elastomeric chains (canines+incisors into an anterior segment, molar+premolars posterior), then reduce residual overjet by retracting incisors as in a first-premolar-extraction case. Continue extraoral force until an intact maxillary arch is achieved.

Fixed Functional Appliances for Adolescent Growth Modification

  • With a Herbst/modern variant, maxillary space opening rarely occurs. Bond the available teeth (canines + incisors both arches, maxillary but usually not mandibular premolars) → align/stabilize lower incisors during molar correction and ease the transition to a regular fixed appliance (usually after ~12 months of Herbst).
Links Ch 14 These approaches aren't mutually exclusive — but even successful growth modification typically gives only a partial correction of a full-cusp Class II/III; the rest is tooth movement.

II Class II Camouflage

When facial appearance is satisfactory with reasonable jaw relationships — three ways to correct with tooth movement.

1 · Distal Movement of Upper Molars

  • Skeletal anchorage (miniplates at the zygomatic base or linked palatal screws — not alveolar screws) is now the most effective way to distalize. With headgear, significant distal movement happens mainly in patients with vertical growth/eruption that lets molars tip distally — without it, hard to get more than 2–3 mm unless second molars are extracted. With skeletal anchorage above the roots, 4–6 mm is possible (major distalization may need second-molar extraction → remove third molars early).
  • In mild-moderate skeletal Class II the upper molars are usually rotated mesially around the lingual root — just correcting the rotation moves the occlusion toward Class I (the first step in Class II treatment).
  • Headgear & Class II elastics (low-pull): >2 mm distal first-molar movement only with simultaneous extrusion (acceptable with ramus growth, else unfavorable down-back rotation). High-pull isn't very effective at distalizing. Class II elastics with a sliding jig can push molars distally (the original Tweed mainstay) — risk of more lower-tooth mesial movement than upper distal. The modern sliding-jig variant is the Carriere Motion appliance Fig 16.18; its main use is to accentuate molar rotation as part of correcting the relationship (no bodily distal movement expected).
  • Skeletal anchorage options:
    • Palatal (pendulum appliance) Fig 16.19 — best example; mostly well tolerated, but palatal-tissue contact can irritate, and however molars are distalized they must be held while the other teeth retract.
    • Miniplate — works as direct anchorage to distalize, then indirect to stabilize while incisors retract. Alveolar bone screws are no longer recommended (must be repositioned; single-screw failure risk).
    • Palatal bone screw — the anterior palate is the best location (thick, dense bone); indirect anchorage from two small screws either side of the suture is adequate.
  • With well-formed maxillary third molars, extracting the second molars is better than it sounds — thirds erupt into the space nicely, bringing bone (75–80% chance). Occasionally unilateral distalization is needed — unilateral cervical headgear works, but skeletal anchorage is preferred (quicker, easier).
New outcome data (7th) In a sample of 35 Class II patients treated with a first phase of pendulum molar distalization then comprehensive fixed appliances, mean treatment duration was 3.1 ± 0.6 years — useful for setting patient expectations.

2 · Differential AP Tooth Movement Using Extraction Spaces

  • Class II camouflage by upper-first-premolar extraction: maintain the existing Class II molar relationship, closing the space largely by retracting protruding incisors. Anchorage must be reinforced — Class II elastics from the lower arch are specifically contraindicated unless the lower incisors need forward movement (rarely the case).
  • The stabilizing lingual arch mainly prevents molars rotating mesiolingually around the palatal root (secondarily prevents mesial tipping). A straight transpalatal arch is as effective as one with a palatal (Nance) button in preventing rotation Fig 16.23 — the slightly better stabilization isn't worth the tissue irritation. (True when stabilizing molars; not when stabilizing premolars, as in molar distalization.)
  • J-hook headgear for direct incisor retraction is no longer recommended — too few hours / too much force (unfavorable force system) and significant binding/friction in the headgear mechanism itself. Retracting the six anteriors usually needs only a single bone screw between 2nd premolar & 1st molar; in adolescents, TADs are necessary only when maximum retraction with no incisor elongation is desired (more an adult situation).
  • All four first premolars: best control with the segmented arch technique (purpose-made space-closing springs). Upper 4s + lower 5s: a common edgewise approach that alters segment anchorage values and simplifies differential closure with a continuous arch.
  • When a second premolar is congenitally missing and a retained second primary molar is to be extracted (wide space → ridge resorbs before closure): remove only the distal root first (calcium-hydroxide pulpotomy + temp restoration), bring the permanent tooth halfway, then extract the rest and finish closure.

3 · Nonextraction Correction With Interarch Elastics

  • Without extraction space, Class II elastics correct molars largely by mesial movement of the mandibular arch (little maxillary distalization) and can over-procline lower incisors. With a well-fitting rectangular lower wire, ~250 gm/side displaces one arch on the other (half that with a lighter round wire). Including the lower second molars and hooking elastics to a mesial hook there boosts anchorage and gives a more horizontal pull.
  • Class II elastics add a vertical force Fig 16.26 — contraindicated in nongrowing patients who can't tolerate some down-back mandibular rotation. Occlusal-plane rotation aids the correction, but maxillary-incisor extrusion can be unsightly. They may give results that look good on casts yet are less satisfactory in skeletal/facial terms. Using them for 3–4 months at the end of treatment for good interdigitation is often acceptable.
Class III Camouflage
  • Class III elastics also have a strong extrusive component (elongate upper molars + lower incisors) Fig 16.26. In a short-face patient with a large mandible, down-back rotation can help (within limits).
  • Retracting lower incisors makes the chin look more prominent — so extraction of mandibular firsts + maxillary seconds with Class III elastics is rarely a good plan in patients of European descent (may suit Asian patients who often have lower-incisor protrusion).
  • A better camouflage for European descent with moderate Class III: extract one lower incisor (prevents major lower retraction) while moving the maxillary incisors facially with some tipping — upright lower + proclined upper incisors often occlude well despite the apparent tooth-size issue, but always do a set-up (digital or plaster) before committing to a lower-incisor extraction. Alternatively, remove mandibular premolars while carefully controlling lower-incisor retraction.
  • For Asian late-adolescent Class III with major lower-incisor protrusion, skeletal anchorage to move the whole lower arch posteriorly can be very helpful.
